transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Doctor. Well, I came in because I just can’t seem to get anything in order anymore. It's gotten completely out of hand. 

My kitchen table is just covered in piles of things—my husband’s appointment papers, flyers from church, notes from the senior center, and all these half-finished lists I make. I just sit down at the table looking at it all, and I don't know which thing to do first. I get so stuck trying to figure it out that... well, before I know it, the whole day is just gone.
How long has this difficulty with organizing and getting things done been going on?

Well, it's been causing this much trouble for... I'd say about a year and three months now. That's right around the time my husband started needing regular help with his appointments and just his daily arrangements in general.
Besides feeling stuck and frustrated about the organizing, how has your mood been overall during this past year? Have you been feeling sad, down, or depressed?

No, I wouldn't say I've been feeling depressed or sad. I mean... I get upset with myself, of course, because I can't seem to manage things the way I should, but it's not a deep sadness or anything like that. My mood is generally fine. I'm really just frustrated by the mess and not being able to figure out what needs doing.
Have you noticed any changes in your memory, or do you have trouble concentrating or thinking clearly—separate from just the organizational frustration?

No, I haven't really noticed any memory problems. I mean, I remember my husband's appointments and the things that happen day to day. And as for concentrating... well, it's not that I can't think clearly in general. It's just when I look at all those papers and try to decide what to do. Other than that, my thinking feels pretty much the same as it always has.
Has your husband or anyone else close to you noticed that you seem more forgetful or confused than you used to be, or have they commented on changes in your thinking?

No, nobody has said anything like that to me. My husband hasn't mentioned me being confused or forgetful, and neither has anyone else. Like I said, I remember everything just fine. It's really just the organizing that's the problem, not my memory.

When you're sitting at that table looking at all the papers, do you notice your heart racing, sweating, or other physical sensations like tension in your body? And do you find yourself worrying a lot about things in general, not just the organizing?

No, I don't get any of that. My heart doesn't race, and I don't get sweaty or tense or anything. I just get... stuck. And I don't really worry a lot about other things, either. It's just those papers and trying to figure out where to put them that bothers me.

When you need to do other things in your daily life—like cooking a meal, paying bills, or getting ready to go somewhere—do you find yourself getting stuck the same way you do with those papers at the table, or is it really just the organizing of papers that causes this problem?

Well, it's not just the papers, actually. Now that you mention it, I guess I do get stuck or just... let things slip in other areas too. 

I mean, I've missed returning phone calls, and I've definitely left bills sitting under a stack of mail instead of just paying them. I've forgotten to run errands I promised my daughter I’d do for her. And... well, more than once I've realized way too late that I never actually called to confirm one of my husband’s appointments, even though I knew about it. So, no, it's not just the organizing. It seems to happen with a lot of everyday things.

Have you noticed that you have more difficulty learning new information or recalling things you learned in the past year or so—for example, having trouble remembering conversations you had, or forgetting things people told you that you would normally remember?

No, I haven't noticed anything like that. I don't have trouble learning new things, and I remember conversations just fine. If someone tells me something, I remember it. My memory really isn't the issue at all.

Before this year started, would you say you were able to organize and manage all these kinds of tasks—like keeping track of papers, remembering to make calls, paying bills on time—without any trouble at all? Or have you actually noticed a real change in your ability to do these things compared to how you used to be?

Well, there's definitely been a change. I used to handle all of that just fine. It really started getting this bad... I'd say about a year and three months ago. That's when my husband started needing regular help with his appointments and his daily arrangements. Since then, it's just been causing me all this trouble.

Around the time this started—about a year and three months ago—did you have any head injuries, falls, a stroke, or any serious medical illness or surgery? Or have you had any significant changes in your health around that time?

No, nothing like that. I haven't had any head injuries or falls, and I definitely haven't had a stroke or any major surgeries. My health has been pretty stable, really. The only big change around that time was just... well, my husband needing more help. But physically, my health hasn't changed at all.

Have you noticed any difficulty with words—like trouble finding the right word when you're talking, or trouble understanding what people are saying to you—or any problems with your balance or coordination since this started about a year and three months ago?

No, I haven't had any trouble with words. I can still talk just fine, and I understand people perfectly well. And my balance is normal too—no problems walking or coordinating things. It's really just the organizing and keeping track of everything that's been so hard lately.

Over this past year and three months, while you've been helping your husband more, have you felt emotionally overwhelmed, exhausted, or burnt out by the caregiving responsibilities? Or have there been any other major stressful events or losses in your life during that time?

Well, no, not really. I mean, sure, it's a bit more work making sure he gets where he needs to go, but I wouldn't say I feel overwhelmed or burnt out by it. It's just part of life, you know? And no, there haven't been any other major stresses or losses or anything like that. Everything else has been pretty quiet, honestly.

When you think about activities you used to enjoy—hobbies, time with friends or family, things that brought you pleasure—do you still feel interested in doing those things, or has your interest in them changed or faded over this past year?

No, I still enjoy all of that. I still love seeing my grandkids and getting together with my friends for lunch. My interest hasn't faded at all. I just... I forget to call them back to set things up, or I lose track of time and show up late. But I still want to do those things just as much as I always have.

Over this past year and three months, have you noticed any changes in your sleep—like sleeping more or less than usual, or trouble falling asleep or staying asleep? And what about your appetite or energy level—have those changed at all?

No, my sleep has been about the same. I fall asleep fine and usually sleep through the night. And my appetite hasn't changed either—I'm still eating normally. As for my energy... I mean, I feel like I have a normal amount of energy for someone my age. I don't feel physically tired all the time, just... frustrated, I guess, with how scattered I am. But physically, my sleep, appetite, and energy are all fine.

Looking back before your husband needed help—say, two or three years ago—did you find it just as easy to organize papers, keep track of tasks, and manage multiple things at once? Or is this difficulty with task initiation and organization something that's truly new since about a year and three months ago?

Well, honestly, it's not completely new. I mean, it's definitely worse now with all the extra things I have to keep track of for him, but... I've always struggled with this kind of thing, even going way back. 

I remember even when I was a little girl, my teachers would write on my report cards that I was bright but careless. I was always forgetting my books or my homework, and they constantly had to remind me to finish my seatwork before I was allowed to go outside. So, I guess I've always been a bit scattered, it's just that I used to have systems that worked well enough, and now... now those systems just aren't holding up.

When you had those systems that worked well enough in the past—before your husband needed help—were you able to manage your work, household responsibilities, and personal life without much difficulty? Or were you still struggling back then, just in ways that didn't matter as much because you had fewer things to keep track of?

Well, back then, I think I just had fewer things to juggle, so my little struggles didn't cause major problems. I could get by. But lately, it's... it's really become a real problem. 

It's actually affecting a lot of my life right now. I recently had to give up leading a big event at the senior center because I just couldn't keep all the details organized anymore. And at home... well, my daughter has actually started double-checking the bills and my appointments. She stepped in because she just doesn't trust that I can keep everything straight on my own anymore. So, yes, the struggle is much, much worse now than it ever was back then.

Growing up as a child and through your teenage years and into adulthood, before your husband needed help, did people—like your parents, teachers, or bosses—regularly comment that you were scattered, forgetful, or didn't finish things you started? Or was it really just your teachers in elementary school who noticed that?

I don't really remember it being a big issue beyond those early school years. I mean, maybe my parents said something here or there, but it wasn't a constant thing. And in my jobs over the years, nobody ever pulled me aside to say I was dropping the ball or anything like that. It was mostly just those elementary school report cards that stand out in my mind.

When you were in your twenties, thirties, and forties—before your husband needed help—did you find yourself frequently losing things, having trouble waiting your turn in conversations, interrupting people, or acting without thinking? Or was it really just the organizing and forgetfulness that was an issue for you?

No, I wouldn't say I had trouble with those things. I mean, I wasn't blurting things out or interrupting people, and I didn't have a problem waiting my turn. I've always been pretty patient in that way. It was really just the... the forgetfulness and the scattered feeling, like we talked about. The organizing things. But no, not the other things you mentioned.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with executive dysfunction (task initiation, organization, planning difficulties) that has acutely worsened over the past 15 months coinciding with increased caregiving demands for her husband. While she has lifelong mild organizational challenges (documented in childhood report cards), the significant functional decline is recent and situational rather than developmental. The absence of cognitive impairment (normal memory, concentration, language, and comprehension), absence of neurological signs (normal balance, coordination, speech), normal mood, and lack of medical/neurological etiology make this best classified as F06.8 (Other specified mental disorder due to known physiological condition) or a stress-related adjustment in executive functioning. The acute worsening in response to psychosocial stressor (increased caregiving burden) with measurable functional impairment (gave up senior center leadership role, daughter now managing finances) supports this classification.
